I'm 48 years old, farming in Anzhai Township, Quzhou County. I have 5 mu of flat land on the North China Plain — all good soil, irrigated from the village well. I finished middle school, so I can read the labels on fertilizer bags and keep my own accounts, but I don't trust fancy new methods I don't understand.

It is late April now. My winter wheat went in last October, and I already gave it the overwinter irrigation before the freeze. The crop is at jointing stage and looks green enough. Next week, when the weather clears, I will topdress with urea — I always do this at jointing, and again if needed at heading. I will irrigate three more times before harvest: jointing, heading, and grain filling. I rotary-tilled before last autumn's sowing, and I sow improved wheat seed — not the old traditional types, but nothing too fancy either. I put down basal compound fertilizer at sowing and topdress twice. Four pesticide sprays in total: twice for aphids, once for weeds, and once for rust. I expect about 500 kg per mu if the weather holds.

Come early June, as soon as the wheat comes off, I will plant summer maize on the same land — no-tillage, straight into the stubble with a drill. I buy hybrid maize seed from the co-op, usually something like Nongda 372. Hybrid seed costs more, but the yield is worth it. I spread basal compound fertilizer at planting and side-dress with urea at the V6 stage. Two irrigations: one when the crop is knee-high, one at tasseling. Three pesticide applications — insecticide twice and herbicide once. I expect around 600 kg per mu of maize.

I thought about planting cotton on a piece of it — I know some neighbors who do — but cotton needs a dozen pesticide sprays and too much hand labor. My back is not what it used to be. Wheat and maize are stable. The grain station buys wheat at a fair price, and the feed mill takes the maize. No haggling, no surprises. That is how I have always done it, and that is how I will do it this year.
